speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Minister Desmond Lee will speak on the relief for the construction and property sectors, found in the new Parts 11 to 13 introduced by this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Today, new temporary measures have been tabled before this House.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Before I take the House through the key features, allow me first to explain why there is a need for these further measures and the broad architecture of the proposed amendments as they are tabled in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The global toll stands today, at about 45 million infections and over 1.1 million deaths, across over 160 countries. 21 October – less than two weeks ago – saw the highest total infections reported in a single day across the world.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A second wave of COVID-19 is surging across Europe.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: France, Germany and most recently, the UK, are now in lockdown.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Infections in the US are trending toward a third peak, and just last week, saw a record for the highest number of cases in a single day.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: COVID-19 is staggering in scale and unprecedented in the way, it has affected almost every aspect of our daily lives.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The way we work, the way we go to school, the way we transact business and even the way we greet each other – we no longer shake hands!

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When we pause to reflect and compare our lives and our daily routines now, compared to where it was eight to nine months ago, we see what a drastically different world we live in today.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have managed to do quite well in terms of treating the sick and keeping the number of deaths low.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, as an international trade hub, we cannot escape the global economic disruption caused by COVID-19 restrictions and border restrictions around the world.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And indeed, for Singapore, we are in our worst recession since Independence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Our GDP is forecast to shrink by 5% to 7% this year.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: MAS predicts that Singapore's recovery will be more protracted than in previous crises and uneven across different sectors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In a corresponding manner, unprecedented Government relief has been provided, to help businesses weather the storm and also to protect jobs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That shows the extent of the measures that the Government has so far introduced.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Measures were also enacted, to deal with the contractual aspect, as Members would know.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In April this year, my Ministry enacted a temporary legal circuit breaker.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We did that practically on the eve of the circuit breaker in April this year. "COVID 1" provided for a moratorium on legal and enforcement actions, for prescribed contracts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Over 8,000 Notifications for Relief were filed and they were filed to invoke the moratorium from April this year. "COVID 1" also raised the debt thresholds for bankruptcy and insolvency to help people avert those consequences as far as possible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Bankruptcy and insolvency applications have consequently dropped significantly, to half or less compared to the first quarter of 2020, since the measure was introduced.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: June saw the introduction of "COVID 2" to give SME tenants immediate rental relief.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The relief has worked as intended and in September I updated Parliament on the impact of these measures.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They have been a crucial lifeline for many businesses.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: One beneficiary of the Act likened it to a parachute, stopping the free fall, helping affected businesses land safely – so still dropping, but with some measure of resistance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This has softened the impact of the pandemic on the economy as a whole and prevented a precipitous increase in defaults on contracts, insolvencies, litigation and consequently, loss of jobs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, we cannot allow or afford for these relief measures to continue, indefinitely.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will risk sustaining businesses that are no longer viable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It would trap, and lock away, precious economic capacity, such as workers or property and assets.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This, in the longer term would be damaging for our economy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng said as well in October, that for the economy to recover, support must evolve and it must go from resuscitate, to rejuvenate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is the key principle behind why this Bill has been proposed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The existing Government support will eventually have to taper off.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The "COVID 1" moratorium should also not be prolonged.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The moratorium holds enforcement actions at bay, as Members know, but it does not stop debts from being incurred as businesses continue and as they continue to perform on contracts entered into.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As announced on 12 October, we have extended the moratorium for a short period of time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The extension for these contracts was for one month, in anticipation of the present Bill being introduced at this sitting.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Businesses have been feeling the impact of COVID-19 since February and in some cases, possibly before that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In April and May, the circuit breaker was implemented.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This was necessary to break the chain of COVID-19 infections and transmissions and to flatten the curve.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But this was an especially painful period for businesses.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Many lost two months of revenue and the impact continues to be felt even some time after the end of circuit breaker.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Due to the impact on their cash-flow, many businesses started accumulating arrears.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Through the Phase Two re-opening, the Government has been carefully monitoring the evolving situation, to see if further relief is needed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members would know that there has been a modest recovery – uneven and modest.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, COVID-19 restrictions cannot be completely lifted as we move cautiously into Phase Three, as announced by the Multi-Ministry Task Force about two weeks ago.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will also affect the F&B and retail stores and transportation workers that rely on tourist spending.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, foot traffic remains reduced, especially in the CBD areas where many still continue to work from home.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Third, retail and F&B outlets must comply with mandatory safe management measures.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Fourth, some businesses are not even permitted to operate at all and this may continue for quite a while.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Those have not been able to operate even now.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Many businesses will be forced to operate in unfavourable conditions in the COVID scenario and in fact, including the immediate post-COVID period for an extended period of time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In a survey by the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry or SCCCI from mid-June to early August this year, they found that half of the respondents said that COVID-19 had a major impact on their business models.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Respondents had experienced a substantial average decline in revenue compared to 2019, without a proportionate decline in business costs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Over 80% of them do not expect business to recover to pre-COVID-19 levels in the next year.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And 58% indicated that they were worried that they will not be able to generate sufficient revenues to even cover their costs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Nightlife businesses especially, are in a difficult situation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And close to 40% said they would definitely, permanently shut down That is why the Government has rolled out specific, targeted support for the worst hit areas.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For the tourism, aviation, arts and sports sectors, the relevant Ministries have, to-date, announced specific support packages for them as well, including grants to help with them with the immediate cash flow difficulties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They should be reallocating resources to more productive uses, rather than being stuck in a prolonged, painful and unproductive struggle, when circumstances, business assumptions have clearly changed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, some businesses, particularly the smaller ones, face obstacles in doing so.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And let me just share an example to illustrate the point with Members.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A tenant wrote to MinLaw that his tenant's lease was for a period ending in October 2021.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The rent was approximately $9,000 per month, something that he entered into before COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Safe management barriers have been erected near his shops.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The tenant's earnings dropped to only $3,000 and even after the Phase Two reopening, the pick-up in footfall has been slow, and clearly, unlikely to return to pre-COVID levels.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: He clearly cannot continue at this rate until October 2021.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I think this is a story which many of the Members in this House would find some resonance with.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The tenant approached the landlord, hoping to negotiate a temporary reduction until the situation improves.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If he could only get a rent reduction for a period of time, he could also free up some resources to transform his business or do what was needed to survive.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, in this particular case, the landlord refused to entertain discussions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the other hand, if the tenant chooses to terminate the contract before his lease ends next year, over a 12-month period, he will have to pay substantial damages for termination.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And that is calculated on the unexpired portion of the lease period.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: He is therefore stuck in this position and continues to bleed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If nothing changes, it is likely that he will breach the tenancy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If the arrears or compensation for termination is not paid, parties could then end up litigation and the tenant might then end up insolvent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That said, we are at the same time also aware of many enlightened landlords.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Many of them have proactively approached the tenants to offer relief or vary the terms of the tenancy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They have renegotiated them, on new terms to help the tenants at least tide over this period of time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, for the many businesses suffering from the lasting economic effects of COVID-19, it really is a simple question in some ways.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Will their counterparties work with them to help them adapt to their business models, restructure the arrangements, possibly downscale or pivot to a different area?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If they cannot get the counterparties to work with them and they are looking at meeting pre-COVID-19 obligations in a COVID-19 economy, then they are heading inevitably for at least a significantly curtailed cashflow, possibly insolvency, and very likely, litigation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This latter scenario is not in the interest of parties nor indeed in the interest of the greater overall good of our economy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If these businesses close down, they will likely be under a mountain of debt.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is not good for the counterparty either because it is unlikely to be able to recover the full debt.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Jobs will be lost, while businesses and creditors tussle over in insolvency or litigation proceedings in Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, to ensure that these businesses do not get stuck in a limbo in a situation where they can neither find it feasible to continue in the present trajectory on the current cash flow and assumptions, nor to terminate and then bear the brunt of the financial impact of that termination.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The second is to have a situation where resources are instead quickly unlocked for more productive ventures in the new operating environment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is the broad objective of these two Bills.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In this respect, Part 10 of the Bill puts in place a realignment framework or we call it the Re-Align Framework for parties to have new alignment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It will help businesses to realign the contractual obligations to the new business reality.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The two measures are separate but complementary, as Members will see.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will take the House first through the Re-Align Framework and subsequently the Simplified Insolvency Programme.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I wish to emphasise that this is not a step that has been taken lightly and we have very carefully considered both the implications as well as the scope of this framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The nub of the problem for the mall tenant that I took the Members through is that he has entered into a contract pre-COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The business environment and assumptions that he had then is very different today.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Now, when all these assumptions are different, he is bound to a set of obligations that were designed at a very different time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And while business is not stagnant, no one could have predicted that the environment would have changed so dramatically, drastically and fundamentally in such a short period of time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For the businesses that are not permitted to resume operations, which I have sketched out earlier, the situation would be even more dire.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Just to give one example of many, I will share an appeal we received from a nightclub owner.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: He had been prohibited from operating since March this year, as is the case for the nightlife industry as a whole.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Its lease continues to run due to expire only in March 2021.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Pivoting to another business model like F&B is possible, but will be difficult.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The premises themselves have no kitchen and the nightclub's workers have returned to their home countries.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Its manager cannot today enter Singapore to come back to work.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The owner is fearful of terminating the lease due to the termination penalties that I sketched out earlier, but with each passing month, the dilemma I think is clear to see.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For suppliers of goods and services, their costs may have skyrocketed and the price that they are contractually bound to pay for the goods and services no longer covers their cost.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But the impact of COVID-19 has also been sudden, widespread and deep.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And whilst some large businesses might be able to absorb the shocks like this, for many businesses, it will be unsustainable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Our first prong, the Re-Align Framework, therefore deals with contracts entered into when the world was a very different place.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The problem, Sir, that needs to be addressed would be as follows.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In relation to businesses trying to meet obligations in a very different circumstances, the contracts in this scenario will need to be realigned.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It will not happen on its own for a number of reasons.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, counterparties may refuse to renegotiate the terms of the contracts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is now a familiar story and I have outlined some examples.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This also commonly arises with the smaller businesses, with less leverage and negotiating power.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, you take the examples that I have highlighted earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is going to be very difficult for a small business – one of maybe several that the counterparty is dealing with, to go back and seek a renegotiation of terms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Here, I think it would be useful to reiterate what Minister Shanmugam had said when this Act was first enacted in April; in these critical times, everyone should take a collective approach.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is not the time to be circling the wagons, taking all that a business can give until they go bust, in the name of exacting contractual rights.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But they are often deterred by the risk of having to pay substantial damages for terminating the contracts early.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Again, in the manner which I have outlined earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Third, the existing recourse that may be available in such situations, may be out of reach and difficult for these struggling businesses to access.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Depending on the facts of the case, some businesses may already have recourse to the doctrine of frustration in Singapore law to discharge their contracts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Under this doctrine, parties are discharged from further performance of their contractual obligations where it can be shown that there is an unforeseeable, supervening event that occurs after the contract was entered into.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The event is not the fault of either party and it renders the performance of the obligations fundamentally different from what the parties had envisaged.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, as I am sure Members here will know, if there is a dispute, businesses will end up spending precious resources: time, effort, money in Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The outcome could also be uncertain and maybe also uneven in the context of different businesses, depending on the facts of each case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it is also difficult to predict how the Courts may rule in one case to another.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For a business already bleeding, the prospect of going to Court to argue these points can be daunting and it is also unproductive for parties to spend the resources in this fashion.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is worth noting that these problems with relying on the law of frustration, were highlighted in an op-ed by former Justice VK Rajah and Dean of SMU Law School, Goh Yihan, published in May.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the op-ed, the authors recognised the need for new COVID-19 legislation to overcome these problems.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They suggested borrowing aspects of contract law from civil law jurisdictions, which allow adjustment of contractual obligations where there is a supervening event.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What the above makes clear, Sir, is that if left to the market alone, the necessary realignment of contracts on the new paradigm, in many cases, will probably not happen.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: My Ministry has received requests from businesses seeking fairly substantial and substantive interventions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, they have asked the Government to consider requiring the mandatory reduction in arrears.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That means you go back to the arrears and you just forgive the arrears.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Or second, just having a different way to calculate future rent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What we think would work best is a more measured approach, which I will now go into.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In redesigning the Framework, I would like to outline to the House three key objectives that we have kept to, in designing this framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The first is to sort out the imbalance to give parties the best chance to come together to renegotiate for themselves what is just and fair in their own context.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And we believe that contractual issues between two parties are best sorted out between the parties themselves as far as possible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They know their operating assumptions and their cost positions and they know what innovations could be made to their specific contract, to help them get over this period.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The first aspect is adapted from concepts found in some major civil law countries.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In these civil law jurisdictions, the right of renegotiation is built into the law.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, in France, in Germany and in Japan, parties significantly affected by an intervening event can invoke the right to renegotiate the contract.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And if it is not successful, they can then apply to court to vary the contract.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The second aspect, the "no fault" termination is drawn from principles of frustration.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It extinguishes all prospective obligations but the parties remain liable for all accrued obligations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These consequences in respect of the accrued obligations also apply as a default in this Framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This right to terminate will shift the calculus for the party on the other side – to give it a nudge, to see if a re-negotiated contract would be a better alternative to either termination or litigation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Often, termination is not the answer for both parties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For a tenant, for example, terminating the lease will come with costs, disruption, the impact of relocation and the risk of losing customers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For the landlord, insisting on strict contract rights in some cases might mean a tenant in serious unrecoverable debt, or a vacant unit or, very often, both.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It may be better to temporarily accept slightly reduced rent or find some other mutually workable formula to help the tenant survive and stay on in the tenancy rather than to leave the premises vacant and to incur the cost of finding a new tenant.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There are a myriad ways to work things out, including shifting to a Gross Turnover or GTO model, for example, for rent or taking a lower rent in the initial period and then extending the term of the lease with a higher rent built in at the tail end – a number of different options that parties can look into.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But ultimately, both sides must work out an arrangement that works well for them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The second objective is to keep this relief narrow and limited so as not to unduly trample upon the sanctity of contracts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is a key and fundamental principle that undergirds our legal system.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In line with the Government's policy of respecting the sanctity of contracts, this Framework will therefore be limited in scope in terms of who it helps and what it will do.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will elaborate on that in a moment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The third objective is to ensure that the Framework is accessible, efficient and it has to be relatively simple to invoke and to use.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We want to minimise uncertainty and to help parties realign their contracts efficiently, fairly and, also importantly, quickly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The sooner we are able to do this, the more we are able to deal with uncertainty in the market.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Framework will therefore set out clearly who it applies to, what contracts it covers and what contracts it does not cover, what the default consequences of termination would be if parties were unable to reach an agreement after re-negotiation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it sets out a framework and a fairly clear formula as to what would be considered, should termination take place.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Part 4 of the Second Schedule of the Bill spells out the default consequences that will apply to a contract covered by this Framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Framework is designed to encourage and give the tools to the parties to work out a negotiated resolution for termination on their own as much as possible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is the fourth objective – for parties to work together as far as possible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will now go into the key features of the Framework to explain to Members how this is designed to work.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, let me focus on whom this Framework would help.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I have mentioned earlier, our primary objective is to help the smaller and the micro businesses – give them a bit of a leverage to find some basis to re-negotiate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They have less negotiating power and are most in need of this assistance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We aim to extend help to the spectrum of businesses that fall within the criteria.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will set a revenue threshold which will exclude the larger enterprises that ought to have the sophistication and wherewithal to engage in negotiations with their own counterparties even without the assistance of this Framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We also intend to cover individuals who enter into contracts for a business or trade purposes, such as freelancers or private hire car drivers and also non-profit organisations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, how do we identify those businesses that have been impacted by COVID-19?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This Framework is not intended to help those businesses who might see a cyclical drop or who maybe, in a scenario where the economy has been doing well, they see a drop in their revenue.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is not the target audience of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It will be, however, onerous and impractical to expect a struggling business – especially the very small ones, including the micro businesses – to have to go through a detailed analysis of its own business performance and pull out the factors that would justify its qualification for this relief.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The effects of COVID-19 have been wide ranging, affecting businesses in many direct ways but also in many indirect ways, including disrupting supply chains, weakening consumer demand.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Some may experience one or more of these and it may be uneven as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It will not be feasible to show all the various factors that have led to the revenue fall and further, to prove that these are caused by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Even if it were possible, it would be difficult and it would be a protracted, long-drawn forensic investigation into each measure and then we get into an argument over whether this factor has got how much proportion and what weightage and whether there has been mitigation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: By the time that process is complete, it will likely be that the business will be in deeper trouble and might well be beyond saving at that juncture.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The fall in revenue criteria will be suitably substantial and pegged to a level such that a business that needs it will clearly have been significantly and adversely affected by the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This, in our view, will strike an appropriate balance between sufficiently showing that there has been substantial impact due to COVID-19 and helping businesses that need an efficient and accessible remedy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have been and we remain in consultation with the industry on the precise criteria and we will announce the criteria once it is finalised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will be set out in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, the contract that can benefit from this Framework must meet the following criteria.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The reason for this date is consistent with, and also explained when, we passed "COVID 1".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is the day immediately after MOH significantly stepped up COVID-19 related restrictions and if parties entered into contracts on or after 25 March with knowledge of the changed circumstances, then these circumstances are no longer unforeseeable, which is really the raison d'etre behind these amendments.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next, the Framework will only cover the prescribed contracts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These are commercial contracts that tend to have substantial prospective obligations, which attract substantial damages or penalties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As such, these are the types of contracts that a business will likely want to re-negotiate and restructure.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the legislation covers four main types of contracts for now.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Section 78 of the Bill empowers the Minister to amend the Schedule of Specified Contracts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This power is needed so that there is flexibility, if necessary, to respond to evolving situations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will just very quickly take Members through them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In general, for these contracts, these are significant cost component for many businesses and the SCCCI's survey, which I cited earlier, found that the topmost need amongst respondents was a reduction or a waiver of rent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As with "COVID 1", we have excluded from this category, hire purchase agreements entered into with MAS-regulated banks or finance companies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is because MAS has worked with the financial industry to provide corresponding substantive relief.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They will extend credit relief measures beyond 2020 to support individuals and SMEs who need more time to resume full loan repayments.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These measures include partial deferments of principal repayments until March or June 2021, depending on the sector that the SME is in.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, borrowers that require additional help can approach the banks or finance company for more customised restructuring arrangements.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In that respect, banks and finance companies have recently developed a protocol to facilitate restructuring of loans across different lenders to reduce the need for borrowers to go to the Courts for resolution.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For the avoidance of doubt, a business may invoke this Framework in respect of a contract even if the Government is a party to the contract as long as the contract is a Specified Contract.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Certain contracts will be excluded from the Specified Contracts for various reasons.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have set them out in paragraph 2 of Part 1 of the Second Schedule.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Again, Members can look at Handout 1 for a summary of these exclusions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, contracts with consumers and employees are excluded.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They are dealt with under a customised set of measures for the construction industry.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Minister Desmond Lee will be speaking on this later.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Also excluded are contracts that are uniquely interconnected with other contracts, where the termination may have unforeseen knock-on effects.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Paragraph 1 of Part 1 of the Second Schedule defines a Specified Contract to include contracts that are substantially in the nature of a specified contract.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Not all contracts are neatly defined into one category or another necessarily and there are often contracts that are mixed or multi-faceted.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, a contract for the supply of goods, which is in the whitelist, may well have an element of carriage of goods, which is in the blacklist.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If it is substantially in the nature of the contract for the supply of goods in the whitelist, it will still be covered by the Framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A contract of national interest is defined in section 41(1) of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The contract must be certified as a contract of national interests by the relevant Portfolio Minister.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It must be one where termination is likely to affect the provision of essential service or the ability of a public body to carry out its function – that is the definition.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A list of specified essential services is set out in Part 2 of the Second Schedule and includes water supply services, security emergency services, broadband Internet services and so on – I think Members understand.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Special considerations therefore apply to contracts of national interest.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: An abrupt termination of these contracts can adversely affect national interest.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is set out in Division 6 of Part 10 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In this context, for these contracts, there will be no right to terminate contracts of national interest.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Instead, there will be a right to re-negotiate the pricing under the contract.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If no solution can be found by that negotiation, the party seeking relief can apply to a Specialist Assessor to adjust the price of the contract.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Specialist Assessors will comprise judges and senior judicial officers appointed to the panel by the Chief Justice.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is needed because of the potential complexity, seriousness and, of course, sensitivity of the disputes, which may relate to contracts of national interest.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If Members refer to Handout 2, I have diagrammatically summarised the process, but I will take Members through key aspects.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, this relief will be available for a period of six weeks from the commencement date of this Bill if it is passed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I explained earlier, we do not intervene lightly and when we do so, it will be in a limited way.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The relief is therefore for a short window to prevent a wider disruption.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is in line with the desired outcome, also, of a quick resolution to the matter.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Once the notice is served, there will be a moratorium on legal and enforcement actions for any non-performance of obligations arising after the date of service of the notice.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We hope that parties will use this four-week period productively and – I would say – openly and constructively to engage with each other in good faith to work out suitable and mutually acceptable arrangements for the longer term, for the balance period of a contract.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If the parties are able to successfully re-negotiate that position, then the matter ends there.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Third, however, if the re-negotiation is unsuccessful, the contract will be terminated but with the default consequences set out in Part 4 of the Second Schedule of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These default consequences generally hold the terminating party to all accrued obligations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members can refer to my Handouts 3A to 3D which will illustrate the default consequences that would generally apply for each type of Specified Contract.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If there is subsequently a dispute over the performance of any obligations that a party may remain liable for after the termination, that dispute can be resolved in the Courts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The first relates to an exception for small landlords who might face hardship.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To invoke this exception, the landlord must meet certain eligibility criteria, which will also be prescribed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The landlords that we have in mind for this are those who have invested their small property and rely on the rental for a good proportion of their annual income.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And if the tenant were to terminate the lease in this case, the landlords may be put into a situation of hardship.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Division 3 of Part 10 of the Bill therefore provides that such landlords are entitled to additional compensation if the lease is terminated.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The compensation amount will be determined by an Assessor in accordance with the criteria that is set out in the prescribed subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To clarify, this is not an assessment of damages.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It will not be done as an assessment of damages in the usual sense.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And the small landlord might not be awarded the full damages that he might have had had he taken the matter to Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But he would have to establish that on a different property value.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, given that a tenant who qualifies to invoke this framework is likely to be suffering badly because of COVID-19, there is a chance that the landlord could not have recovered the full amount of damages from the tenant anyway.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, bear that in mind in the context of what I have also outlined in the preamble earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As an alternative option to termination, the Bill also provides a Statutory Repayment Scheme or SRS specifically for these types of contracts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is set out in Division 4 of Part 10 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Once was a business that hire-purchased mini vans to ferry tourists and corporate clients.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Its usual business had ground to a halt.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is now using the vans to do deliveries.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The revenue earned is still not enough for it to fully pay its hire-purchase instalments.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the same time, the finance companies are threatening to re-possess the vans.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And without the vans, obviously, even the new delivery business will fall.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The livelihoods of these hirers depend on the equipment and the vehicles that they hire-purchase.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They are often the sole breadwinners with families who do depend on them to survive and termination in these cases is not really an option for such businesses.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Interest will remain payable on the outstanding arrears, capped at 5% per annum.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And if a party fails to pay any instalment as required by the Schedule, or terminates or repudiates the contract during the period of the repayment period, otherwise they are still offsetting the instalments due, then all outstanding arrears will become immediately repayable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, to ensure the smooth implementation and delivery of the relief to the intended beneficiaries, the relief under the Framework applies to contracts that are terminated from 2 November 2020 when the Bill was introduced.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will prevent a rush of terminations, leading to uncertainty in the market.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This Framework, Sir, is an exceptional, targeted intervention, for extraordinary times.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Rule of Law, which includes respecting the sanctity of contracts, is a foundational value for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We worked with legal experts, considered it carefully, and consulted industry stakeholders such as Singapore Business Federation, the Singapore Nightlife Business Association and other businesses and trade associations, landlords, tenants and banks.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This was not a step that was taken lightly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ultimately, this Framework protects our economy in the longer term by helping businesses overcome barriers to choosing the more economically productive route.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It helps the market to correct and operate as it should.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is also not a concept alien to both the common and civil law traditions where we see that there is a recognition of fairness and that a fundamental unforeseeable change in circumstances that impacts the performance of a contract can justify a change in the contractual environment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This Framework therefore adheres to the principles for intervention by the state in contracts, as set out by Minister Shanmugam in Parliament, when this Act was first introduced in April.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, that the freedom of contract has never been absolute, and even today, there are mandatory laws that can invalidate or override terms of a contract.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In these circumstances, a state may intervene, with reasonable steps of limited duration, to safeguard the economic structure for the common good.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have never before seen such deep and significant impact in any of our past crises, whether it is the Asian Financial Crisis, the Global Financial Crisis, or SARS.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It would ensure that the cash infusions are not drained away because businesses are stuck in their contracts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It will help substantially impacted businesses avoid protracted disputes, re-strategise and, in Deputy Prime Minister's words, to rejuvenate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I understand there may be concerns about knock-on terminations, chain reactions and so on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But let me ask Members to consider the facts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The businesses that we have scoped this to cover are those that had been substantially impacted.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Even without this relief, they face a likelihood of being insolvent, at the minimum, substantial litigation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The duration of this relief is limited and in consequences following the termination, carefully scoped, to ensure as far as possible, fairness for both parties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There are fears the Framework could be used by parties as a convenient escape route to terminate the contracts that some parties might set unreasonable or unacceptable re-negotiation terms to force a termination.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But Members ought to note that, first, this is designed to allow parties to be as flexible as possible in the context of their own contractual environment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I would urge the parties to work together to look this productivey.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And second, whilst we cannot say for everyone and over-generalise, we believe that the vast majority of people and businesses affected by this will act commercially and rationally.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: No rational tenant will choose to exit a tenancy unnecessarily because there is a cost to moving, there is a relocation cost, and moving away from its existing pool of customers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Those who choose to exit will probably generally believe that they have no choice given their business and operating assumptions, and the cost.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But even in those cases, the landlords can engage in discussions to try and understand their difficulties and find a solution, again, using one of the different options that I have outlined earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the situation where there might be a number of parties who seek to attempt to misuse this system, the Assessor system is a check and safeguard against this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Assessor's responsibility is primarily to ensure a fair and just outcome.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In unforeseeable circumstances that are no fault of their own, many businesses will be worried about cutting costs, making ends meet, dealing with impending litigation or maybe insolvency.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And this is a time when we would much rather help those businesses to adapt, to find a new paradigm, find a new operating assumption, to recover, get their businesses back on track and save jobs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In order to fully appreciate how this Bill will help financially distressed companies, assist in saving jobs and strengthen the macro environment for businesses, let me first explain why an effective insolvency framework is important. for the economy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A successful restructuring allows a company to continue as a going concern.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This results in a better outcome for employees, creditors and investors as a whole, by saving jobs and the businesses and giving a lifeline.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Where the business of a company, on the other hand, is no longer viable, then an effective liquidation process realises the company's remaining assets in an orderly fashion and distributes the proceeds to creditors and stakeholders through an effective and transparent collective enforcement mechanism.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This enables the reallocation of resources to other more productive business activities.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It also reduces the number of zombie companies that might exist, those that are unable to generate enough profits to cover their debt-servicing costs and other obligations while the value of their assets dissipates over time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: An efficient liquidation process will reduce the costs of liquidation, and maximise returns to the company's stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is therefore critical that the distressed companies are provided with the necessary statutory framework to either restructure, or to wind down their operations in an effective and orderly manner.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: An efficient and streamlined framework will reduce the complexity and hence the cost and time of doing so for debtors and stakeholders alike.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The purpose of this Bill is to create such a framework, tailored for the micro and small companies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We already have in place, Sir, a progressive and modern insolvency framework in the Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution Act or IRDA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is the fruit of a multi-phase process that has taken about five years to put in place to strengthen our insolvency framework and enhance our position as an international centre for debt restructuring.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This introduced a new differentiated discharge framework that promotes a more rehabilitative regime by giving bankrupts clear targets to work towards so that they can become eligible for discharge.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It puts in place also, a requirement for institutional creditors to appoint private trustees in bankruptcy when making a bankruptcy application.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This encouraged greater engagement by such creditors and also drives creditors to exercise greater financial prudence when granting credit.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In 2017, we introduced ground-breaking amendments to the Companies Act to strengthen the framework even further, introducing super-priority for rescue financing, encouraging fresh funds to assist the debtor through the restructuring proceedings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We enhanced moratoriums to provide breathing room for distressed companies and also put in place pre-packaged schemes of arrangement to fast-track pre-negotiated, pre-agreed restructuring plans.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On 30 July 2020, just a few months ago, the IRDA was commenced and incorporates the relevant provisions from the Bankruptcy Act and the Companies Act, into a single new statute.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Act also builds on the earlier phases of amendments that I have outlined.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Our legislation provides the best features of the world's leading regime.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It also seeks to strike a balance between the different competing stakeholders' interest, enabling companies to restructure successfully whilst at the same time, protecting creditors' rights.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The touch stone of any Singapore restructuring remains the support of its creditors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In any insolvency, it is the creditors who own the company.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A recent restructuring example that I would like to highlight to Members is Swee Hong Limited, a civil engineering contracting firm.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In February 2020, the High Court granted Swee Hong an order to give super-priority status to over US$2 million worth of rescue financing.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This allowed them to continue the business whilst it attempted to restructure.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Seven months later, the proposed scheme of arrangement was approved by more than 90% in number of creditors, representing more than 80% in value, higher than the requisite statutory threshold, and if sanctioned by the Court, the restructuring would allow Swee Hong which was insolvent to continue as a going concern and avert a winding up.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This in turn helps to save the business, keeps jobs not only for Swee Hong but also for many of its counterparties and subcontractors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Whilst the IRDA has facilitated positive results such as Swee Hong, it was not designed with the effects of a global pandemic like COVID-19 in mind.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These are enterprises with annual revenues of less than $1 million and $10 million respectively.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, micro is $1 million, and "small" would be $10 million.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Thus, it is likely that a significant number of financially distressed companies, as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic, are likely to be micro and small companies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have received feedback that these companies, in particular, may still find it financially challenging to apply the provisions under IRDA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, where there is a ready investor prepared to come into the business, or alternatively, where the company is in a position to renegotiate with its creditors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, to wind up the company, where the business has ceased to be viable but in a quick, efficient and low-cost manner.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The proposed amendments seek to provide temporary processes that fit these purposes and benefit stakeholders of the company such as employees and, of course, also the trading counter-parties, creditors and shareholders by reducing the time it would take to either do a restructuring or a liquidation and maximising potential recoveries.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The new processes were developed in consultation with public agencies and stakeholders from the private sector.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This ensures that the framework is able to meet the needs of small and micro businesses.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Separately, the Bill also has one miscellaneous amendment which I will cover at the end, in relation to the licensing framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Simplified Insolvency Programme comprises the restructuring programme and the liquidation programme.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In some ways the process and the formulae for determining who qualifies for both have similarities so I will cover them very briefly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In relation to the application processes for both programmes, the new sections 72B and 250B of the IRDA Bill, the programmes will open for application by eligible companies for a “prescribed period”.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This may be shortened or extended for a period to be determined by the Minister.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Overall, this window for application will be shorter than the overall lifespan of the proposed provisions, which is three years after its commencement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Where any company applies to the Official Receiver under the new sections 72E or 250D under the relevant “prescribed period”, and the Official Receiver assesses the eligibility requirements and are satisfied on the face of the application, then the Official Receiver under the new sections 72G or 250G, will send a notice of the application to the applicant company and all creditors named in the application and, in the case of section 250G, which is for liquidation, also to every contributory or officer named in the application, and publish the notice on the designated website.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To provide flexibility, the figures that I have mentioned to Members may be substituted by the Minister abd prescribed by way of an Order in the Gazette.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Where there is any objection to the acceptance of the applicant into the relevant programme, the Official Receiver must consider the objection and decide whether or not that particular company qualifies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If not, to exclude; if so, then to allow the company to avail itself of the process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The applicant company has to pay a fee and a deposit and this will be used in a way which would defray the costs of the Official Receiver.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In order to provide flexibility to address companies that merit assistance under the programme even if they might miss out on the eligibility requirements, the Minister may direct the Official Receiver, under the new sections 72H or 250H, to send and publish the notice of application and then to accept the applicant into the programme.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Part 5A of the IRDA Bill establishes the simplified restructuring programme and I will just quickly take Members through the most salient provisions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This, as Members might appreciate, is modelled on the existing pre-packaged scheme in section 71 of the existing IRDA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Under the pre-packaged scheme process, a proposed compromise or arrangement is worked out among the company and its creditors but done out of Court, without having to invoke the Court process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You come to an arrangement with your creditors, which is then subsequently submitted to the High Court for approval.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Instead of two applications to the Court required in a typical scheme of arrangement, the pre-package only requires one application.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Upon the acceptance of a company into the simplified debt restructuring programme and before the company is discharged, the company enjoys a statutory moratorium under the new section 72K(1), and amongst others, it restrains the commencement or continuation of any proceedings against the company.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The company is also restrained from disposing of its property under the new 72K(3), unless it is done in good faith and in the ordinary course of its business.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is to ensure that the assets are not dissipated whilst there is a moratorium in place.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Creditors are also prohibited from exercising certain contractual rights under an ipso facto clause under the new section 72T, which applies section 440 which is the ipso facto clause of IRDA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is done with modifications, as appropriate, for smaller companies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This framework balances the interests of the various stakeholders by providing, on the one hand, breathing room via the moratorium to the company but, at the same time, preserving the rights of creditors to have access to the company that has not wrongly and unfairly dissipated its assets.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This Restructuring Advisor will be available to advise the company to prepare its papers and generally to guide the company through this process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, two-thirds in the value of the debts that are owed by the company must approve this scheme.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There is no specific number of creditors required to assent to the scheme, unlike a traditional scheme of arrangement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the thresholds are slightly more relaxed than in the usual scheme of arrangement under 210 of the Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is intended to provide certainty to the company on the default approach towards classification of creditors, given the simpler nature of the debt structure of these micro and small companies and, of course, to avoid potential litigation which sometimes happens in relation to the way in which the company classifies its creditors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Nevertheless, the Court retains overriding discretion under the new section 72M(5) to take into account the agreement or disagreement of any related party, and if the circumstances so require and the result of doing so would be fair and equitable to all creditors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the Court still retains an overriding discretion to do so.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Court may, under the new section 72M(6), without hearing all arguments, grant or dismiss an application, as the case may be; and instead of having the company required to engage counsel, a duly authorised officer of the company may represent the company in the relevant court proceedings without the leave of court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is provided for under the new section 72N.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is not uncommon in many other jurisdictions around the world even for the usual restructuring process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This keeps the process on an even keel and if more time is needed, an application for extension can be sought.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But in the first instance 90 days is being given to enter into the arrangements, and also the limited timeframe is designed not to unfairly prejudice creditors because during that period of time, whilst this is being looked into, there is a moratorium.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Under the general framework, Sir, typically at least three applications are required.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, for the moratorium itself; second, for leave to convene a meeting; and third, for the sanction of the proposed compromise or arrangement and then oftentimes, a financial adviser will also be required.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This simplified process brings it into one single application and, if accepted, the company will enjoy the benefits of the moratorium early on and really only one application would be needed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Under this voluntary winding up, a company is wound up without the need for a Court application to place the company into winding up.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is modelled on the existing creditors’ voluntary winding up process that is already found in the Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Before making an application, the company must pass a special resolution, authorising the making of the application and so on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And upon acceptance of a company into the simplified winding up programme, the voluntary winding up of the company commences at that stage.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Official Receiver may also appoint a qualified person to act as a special manager under section 250M.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The winding up is treated as if it were a creditors’ voluntary winding up, as I mentioned earlier, under section 250K(2).

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The provisions that therefore apply to the creditors' voluntary winding up will also apply in relation to the company, unless they are modified under section 250L and the conditions are set out in section 250L.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A company is discharged from the simplified winding up programme under section 250N – when the company is dissolved; or an order is made by the Court to wind up the company, stay the proceedings or terminate the winding up.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Lastly, the new section 250O sets out the non-exhaustive circumstances in which the Official Receiver, as the liquidator, may apply to the Court under section 124 of the IRDA to wind up the company.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Such circumstances include where the Official Receiver is satisfied that the company either did not meet, or could not meet, or no longer meets the eligibility criteria for the programme.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The provision is not intended to affect the rights of any person entitled to make an application under section 124 of the IRDA for the company in simplified winding up to be wound up under a Court order.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And that also includes the Official Receiver as liquidator.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Currently, one would have to apply to Court or pass a special resolution and convene the necessary meetings, the company would have to seek a liquidator who would have to agree to being appointed, and the creditors may also then appoint a Committee of Inspection to act in respect of the winding up.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In comparison, under this simplified process, the process is commenced once an application is made to the Official Receiver.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If the Official Receiver accepts it, the winding up commences without more.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Official Receiver becomes the liquidator and there will not have to be a Committee of Inspection.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These are in addition to the other features and modifications that I have outlined earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The simplified winding up process is really designed for companies who have taken the view – small and micro businesses who qualify – that it is no longer sustainable to remain in this business.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Rather than have a protracted process where more time, more effort, more costs are put into managing the exit from the business, those companies can avail themselves of this mechanism.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is an amendment that is separate from the Programme.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members who have been in Court and argued this or seen this applied, will know that there have been insolvency professionals who act for companies or creditors in cross-border transactions, cross-border restructurings, and those are one type of professionals that we envisage would come under these exemptions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I have taken Members through the two new measures in both Bills.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These are necessary as a part of a suite of measures that the Government is providing to help businesses and our workforce and, fundamentally, people and jobs emerge stronger from the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In some ways, it is significantly more complex than the earlier "COVID 1" and "COVID 2" in terms of the concept and its scope of application.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We also did not have the luxury of time as a Bill like this would typically have taken some months up to a year to conceptualise and make workable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It was only possible because of the outstanding contributions of many of those who worked very closely and very hard with my Ministry to put this together.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: MTI and ESG, in particular, were always ready to help with ground sensing, with the data, making helpful suggestions to refine our proposals, to scope them carefully and appropriately.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: MAS, too, did the same, contributing their own domain expertise and helping to bring stakeholders on board in explaining the process, explaining the intent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We are indebted to our other colleagues from the other Ministries and agencies like MOT, MCCY, MND, HDB, JTC, MHA and SLA, and of course, MOF, too.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Besides paying for the Bill, they also attended all our meetings and helped us to work out a solution, especially when it came to dealing with contracts of national interest.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I wish to thank in particular, Mr Sushil Nair and Mr Patrick Ang – two private sector lawyers on the committee who have been working with us since "COVID 1".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They gave of their time very generously and they also helped us to not just conceptualise but also draft and redraft the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Along with a judge of the High Court, Justice Kannan Ramesh, their years of legal experience and insights were very much invaluable and a pivotal part of the way in which we were able to produce this Bill in short order.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We consulted with them very closely and we scoped the provisions based on the views that they gave us and the feedback that they gave us, honing our policies and our thinking.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will put their names on record without having to mention them individually.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There is an Annex which will be put into the transcript.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This Bill is the product of not just legal solution but indeed legal innovation that they have helped us with in difficult, complex times.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I wish to thank all of them and place on record the MinLaw's gratitude to all of them for their framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Because of this, we believe that we will have a better chance at emerging stronger from this pandemic, ready to overcome the challenges ahead of us in the mid to longer term.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But the sector, especially construction, has been hit very hard by the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Construction ground to a complete halt during the circuit breaker period.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: After the circuit breaker, projects could not restart immediately as the dormitories took some time to be cleared.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Without any work done, payments were delayed and consultants and builders faced serious cash flow problems.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Border restrictions also disrupted supply chains and some workers being stuck outside Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Within Singapore, many of our migrant workers were locked down in their dormitories due to COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Home buyers and business owners were also impacted as their premises under construction were delayed and many had to make alternative arrangements meanwhile.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As the impact of a total shutdown of construction activity was unprecedented and the situation was evolving very rapidly, we had to have very frequent meetings between agencies and industry associations and ground visits.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This allowed us to better understand ground realities and adjust our restart measures accordingly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To prevent a collapse of the entire industry, we had to intervene very significantly – through providing financial assistance, foreign worker levy waivers and rebates and putting in place legislation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This Bill seeks to provide further support to stakeholders to ensure that no one in the built environment sector has to bear a disproportionate share of the burden brought about by the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, please consider the measures being proposed today not in isolation but as part of a whole series of interventions and trade-offs along the length and breadth of the entire built environment value chain, affecting but at the same time also supporting buyers, developers, consultants, builders, sub-contractors and suppliers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: With these and other measures in place, we hope the sector can adapt and adjust to the new operating environment, recover quickly from the pandemic and preserve industry capacity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Before diving into the provisions of today's Bill that are pertinent to the built environment sector, let me first sketch out the measures that we have already put in place to support main contractors, sub-contractors and suppliers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In addition, the Act also provides a defence against breach of contract and damages due to COVID-19 for the construction and supply contracts that they are parties to.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This means that developers cannot claim damages from their contractors for a delay that is assessed to be due to COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Part 8 of the Act also provides a mechanism for firms to seek relief from additional rental costs that are incurred due to construction delays caused by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This means that contractors who had rented equipment during the circuit breaker but who were unable to use this equipment as no work was on-going can apply for an equitable adjustment of the rental costs that they must pay to the suppliers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Developers have to deal with project delays and the increased costs for their projects.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As projects are delayed, home buyers and businesses may have to incur additional rental and other costs while waiting for their new homes and premises to be ready.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Hence, the Government has also provided relief to developers and purchasers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Developers could not terminate agreements for sale and purchase of property with the buyers on the basis of the buyer's non-payment nor increase interest rates or impose new charges without buyers' agreement during the relief period.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We also capped the late payment interest or charges under agreements for sale and purchase of property.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Together, we have made progress in restarting construction.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We completed the clearance of the dormitories in August this year and since then, COVID-19 infection among our workers in dormitories has come down significantly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On a daily basis, there are very few infection cases, if any.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But to prevent a resurgence, we have also taken measures to strengthen our defence against COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In October 2020, we completed the cohorting of workers in dormitories so they stayed together with colleagues from the same firm instead of mixing with workers from other firms.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are also giving out 450,000 BluePass tokens, which will allow us to better conduct contact tracing of COVID-19-positive cases and to more surgically quarantine those who have been in close contact instead of casting an overly wide quarantine net.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have implemented the BuildSG-COVIDSafe Platform for better worksite access control and data-driven audit and inspection.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While we have made progress, the construction sector is far from being out of the woods.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The threat of resurgence continues to loom and the sector will grind to a halt again if we are not careful.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We also continue to receive feedback that the sector is still facing challenges.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Labour cost has increased due to a lack of supply of new migrant construction workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Projects continue to face delays as productivity has dropped due to the necessary safe management measures in place at construction sites.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, from 7 April to 1 June 2020, construction works stopped for approximately two months due to the circuit breaker period.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, works were further delayed by at least two months as all dormitories were only cleared in early August 2020.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This universal extension of time will reduce the administrative burden for contractors so that they can focus on restarting and ramping up work quickly and safely and adjusting to the new measures required.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For contractors who wish to seek a longer EOT beyond the four months, they can negotiate with developers or rely on contract provisions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Alternatively, contractors can also serve a Notification for Relief on the developer as a defence under section 6 of Part 2 of this Act, to disregard any liquidated damages payable under the contract due to delays.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Next, let me go through Part 8B of the Bill, which will require the built environment value chain – from builders to contractors to sub-contractors, to co-share additional costs due to delays in the project caused by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, some contractors will need to rent machinery like tower cranes for a longer period, as works have been delayed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Bill will allow contractors or sub-contractors to claim part of these costs from their clients through regular progress payment claims.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will ensure contracting parties co-share a fair amount of these additional costs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In cases of disputes, contractors can submit an adjudication application under the existing Building and Construction Industry Security of Payment Act or SOPA framework.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The appointed SOPA adjudicator will be able to determine whether the relief applies, and if it does, he will then determine the amount to be co-shared between the parties.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As I described earlier, developers are also facing difficulties on their end.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
