text: Even as they are required to provide the EOT to contractors and to co-share additional costs of the delay in Parts 8A and 8B respectively, they remain liable to deliver the units to purchasers according to the deadlines set in their sale and purchase agreements entered into prior to the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is in the interest of developers for projects to be completed in a timely manner and they have been working closely with contractors to do so, while ensuring compliance with COVID-safe measures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: However, there may be some instances where they are unable to meet the committed delivery date due to unexpected delays caused by the COVID-19 situation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have been encouraging developers who are unable to meet the date of delivery to first discuss with their purchasers and come to a workable and mutually agreeable arrangement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For developers who are unable to come to an arrangement and require help, the Bill will allow them to seek relief on the date of delivery of possession.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Should the developer need relief of more than four months, they will be required to seek an assessor's determination of the length of construction delay materially due to COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Hence, we want to support purchasers who have had to incur out-of-pocket expenses and costs due to the delay in delivery of the units.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, some purchasers may have had to rent accommodation or find alternative premises during the period of delay.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As such, purchasers may seek reimbursement from the developer for these actual costs, up to a cap of 70% of the original liquidated damages that would have been payable to the purchaser for the delay, based on the terms in the agreement for the purchase of the property.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For HDB flats, purchasers can similarly claim up to 70% of the prescribed LD formula, which will be aligned with that of the formula stated in the Housing Developers Rules for private residential properties.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This allows for co-sharing of such costs between the developer and purchaser.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And if there are any disputes, parties can seek an Assessor’s determination.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The sector has been brought to its knees and is slowly standing up again, adjusting to a totally new operating environment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In this regard, stakeholders of this sector continue to face significant financial, possibly legal burden due to COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Parts 8A to 8C of the Bill will help alleviate the hardship faced by these stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The aim of the amendments is to share the burden amongst the stakeholders while providing relief, to allow us to get through the crisis together.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Beyond this Bill, MND will continue to work with the stakeholders to help the built environment sector recover and preserve industry capacity for us to continue building and improving Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This was later enhanced in the Resilience Budget on 26 March 2020.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, a shop is granted 100% Property Tax Rebate, which is equivalent to approximately 1.2 months of rent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Property owners are also required to fully pass on the benefit of the Rebate to their tenants within the prescribed timelines.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This obligation is provided under Part 6 of this Act and the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) Regulations 2020, or the PT Rebate Regulations, which came into force on 13 May 2020.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Later on, to further support tenants, the Government introduced the rental relief framework.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And that came into force on 31 July 2020.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, the owner of a shop is required to waive up to four months of rent for his eligible tenants, for the period April to July 2020.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And the Government co-shares in this mandated rental waiver, by providing support through the Property Tax Rebate and a Government cash grant.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, for a shop, the support by the Government, through the Rebate and the grant, is about two months, or about half of the four months of rental waiver which the shop owner is required to waive for his eligible tenants.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These regulations are needed to ensure that the property owner will not become unduly worse off by having to pass on the benefit of the Property Tax Rebate to his tenants, on top of the rental waiver that is effected under the rental relief framework.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: To give an illustration of how such an inadvertent consequence may arise, let us assume that there is a change in tenants during the course of the year, with Tenant A occupying the shop premises until July 2020, and then Tenant B comes in, occupying the premises from August 2020 onwards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If Tenant A is a SME, the shop owner is to waive up to four months of rent for Tenant A, from April to July 2020, under the rental relief framework.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The owner should have then fully satisfied his obligation to pass on the benefit of the Property Tax Rebate of about 1.2 months of rent as well as some of the cash grant and he would have satisfied the obligation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But under the existing PT Rebate Regulations, the owner is also required to pass on the benefit of the Property Tax Rebate to Tenant B, pro-rated at about 0.5 month.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And this is not the intended outcome because the owner had already waived four months of rent for Tenant A under the rental relief framework and passed on the benefit of the Property Tax Rebate to Tenant A.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, the owner should not need to pass on any benefit of the Property Tax Rebate to Tenant B.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is why the Bill provides regulations to be made retrospectively, to ensure that this position is maintained.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And if the owner has already passed on the benefit of the Rebate to Tenant B, this Bill will also allow regulations to be made to allow the owner to recover the excess amounts from Tenant B in such circumstances.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So really, the provisions are here just to ensure that the intended policy outcomes are effected and there is no undue burden on property owners.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Details of the regulations will be provided through subsidiary legislation and on IRAS' website when ready.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I declare my interest as a dispute resolution lawyer who handles insolvency matters in the course of my work.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution Act or IRDA which came into effect in July this year is an important reframing and harmonising of the insolvency regime in Singapore, which was previously found largely in the Companies Act and the Bankruptcy Act.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The general principles governing the insolvency regime have been to ensure that all interested parties will have a say in the insolvency process, depending on their interest in the company.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, for solvent companies, the winding up process can be commenced by shareholders.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For insolvent companies, typically, it is the creditors that commence the winding up process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This process, generally, requires public notification and an order by the Court.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Interested parties can appear in Court and either object to or be heard in the process if they wished.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While many envision insolvency as a creditor-driven process, the insolvency process also provides important protections for debtors, including protections like moratoriums on enforcement actions and, in some cases, this will even permit the companies to operate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, the current insolvency regime includes schemes of arrangement or judicial management systems which allow companies to continue to be run.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This has the important benefit of preserving jobs for employees while also allowing creditors better recovery than a fire sale of assets.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The main downside of this process is that it can be costly and, for many small companies, especially those that have financial difficulties, the cost of such a process can be prohibitive.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, for small companies, they generally do not commence the debt restructuring process themselves and are often led into winding up or insolvency when one of their creditors finally decides to wind-up the company.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Before that, it is likely that the creditors would have seized and sold whatever assets they could to satisfy their debts.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, what would be left may well be a rump company.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This should not be difficult to do if the company has a few creditors and only a few shareholders, which is the case for many smaller companies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This process may seem "rough and ready" compared to the insolvency process in the Courts.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But I think it is a fair trade-off for lower costs and efficiency.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The onus will be on company officers to ensure proper disclosures have been made in the course of the application process and all creditors will receive notification of the process and can participate if they wish.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This, to me, is a very practical solution and I think it will work well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Of course, for this process to work effectively, the OA must have enough capacity to meet a caseload that would previously have been handled by the Courts and make decisions quickly as a moratorium can make the difference between life and death for small companies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One last point, as I note that the main driver for these amendments is the COVID-19 pandemic and the need to put in place urgent measures to help businesses survive during this period.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would suggest that if this process proves efficient and effective, we should consider making these amendments a permanent feature of our legislation rather than just a temporary measure for these times.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the second part of my speech, I will address the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) (Amendment No 3) Bill.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is actually the fourth Bill in relation to COVID-19 put forward by MinLaw.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: COVID-19 has had a devastating impact on our economy, and industries like aviation, tourism, oil & gas and retail continue to remain under water.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Our national carrier, Singapore Airlines, is on life support and, recently, Robinson's, once our flagship retail store, announced its plans to close its remaining stores in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While many sectors have reopened, some do not have clarity on the horizon.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This includes sectors like tourism, aviation and nightlife-related businesses.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But before doing that, they can actually trigger a process to renegotiate contracts and, in particular, paying slight rental obligations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This, to me, is actually a very powerful mechanism, if we look at it from the prism of businesses that are affected.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, businesses may be locked into long-term contracts and this may be difficult for them to get out of.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, on the one hand, they cannot terminate the contracts if they are locked in, say, a two-year lease.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But on the other hand, because their business is completely impacted, they have no way of making those payments.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think this is a very powerful mechanism to help what we expect will be the weaker party in the contract, the one that is locked into unfavourable terms.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I hope that all businesses act in the spirit of this legislation and actually renegotiate their obligations, rather than end up at the default termination if they do not.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But I should also mention while this mechanism is likely to give many smaller operators greater leeway in negotiations, it is also important that we do not forget that landlords, too, are likely to be affected by this range of measures.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: You may have big landlords all the way to small landlords.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While we may not look at big landlords very favourably, it is also important to understand that many big landlords, especially the corporate ones, may have obligations to lenders who are financing their operations, they have employees to pay for.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Of course, for smaller landlords, it is far easier to understand their plight.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Some of them may have heavily leveraged to pay for properties and may require rentals to pay off their loans.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, these landlords may also be facing difficulties.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Retirees are another group of people who may have investment properties and rely on rental income to pay for their retirement.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Related to this, I have two questions for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If so, what should landlords do in this situation?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Notwithstanding the questions I have raised, I believe this is a well thought through and necessary Bill that helps many businesses to continue or at least exit with less difficulty.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The amendments are essential refinements in our response to the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The COVID-19 Temporary Relief Act was described by Minister Shanmugam as a Noah’s Ark, with many moving parts to bring as many as possible to higher ground.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The points I would like to raise today are on the temporary provisions regarding bankruptcy and insolvency.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Two, for these same badly hit sectors and, hopefully, even beyond, I also propose temporarily removing some of the penalties for directors of insolvent companies affected by the pandemic, so that they can meaningfully contribute to the re-birth and restart of their sectors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I applaud Part 2 of the Temporary Relief Act because it gives individuals and businesses breathing space.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This was done by increasing the bankruptcy and insolvency limits as well as to extend the minimum number of days, from serving of a statutory demand, to serving notice of bankruptcy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As of today, we have made excellent progress in controlling the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: More and more of our economy is operating closer to normal, and Part 2 has largely served its purpose.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: However, there are compelling reasons to restore Part 2 for our worst hit sectors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: One, as we move towards Phase Three, many of these badly hit sectors could become financially viable again as safe-distancing measures get redefined.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: With support, many insolvent companies in these sectors may not need to go down that path.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Two, while the past six months have created a valuable breathing space, a large amount of effort and time was spent on clarifying the terms, such as the rental relief details and on refining the powers of the assessors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It is only until recently – based on my conversations with the SMEs – that creditors and debtors are better able to work together to support SMEs through this crisis.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: So, extending the runway will be beneficial and in Singapore’s best interests.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Three, for the badly hit sectors, our economic agencies will need more time to identify the way forward, to find higher ground for companies in those sectors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As an example, a clear way forward for some well-managed companies in these sectors would be to re-capitalise or to pivot to a new direction.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But we have to ask ourselves are we giving the present Government schemes sufficient time to take effect, to allow them to make this happen?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Is the equity funding part of our business eco-system ready to step up?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Do investors or white knights have enough time to complete their due diligence?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I believe that more time is needed for the Government to work with these sectors to reinvent themselves.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Four, we have a moral obligation to do even more to support these sectors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Even though we now have low number of local infections, we have extensive safe distancing measures because we need to keep our economy open.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: That means running the risk of imported cases as the situation deteriorates in many parts of the world.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: To counter balance the risk, we are continuing with strong curbs in the events, entertainment and high-end F&B activities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Firms in these sectors are paying the ultimate price of our collective efforts to fight COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: They deserve more time to work with creditors to find a way forward.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Five, many of our national retraining and reskilling efforts are under strain from the recent spike in unemployment and we need to give them more time to ramp up.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: By forestalling bankruptcies and insolvencies, we can buy MOM, WSG and E2I more time to help displaced workers find new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The rise and fall of companies are part of any economic downturn and restructuring.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In a normal downturn, when old firms fade away, new firms will seek new opportunities funded by new capital and the economy will rise again.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But for the badly hit sectors, what we have is not a normal downturn.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This is a mass extinction event, especially for SMEs – a global killer so to speak.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Of course, many of these sectors, especially the SMEs, will need to do things differently, or at least continue operating with restrictions for a prolonged period of time.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But when conditions allow for re-emergence of these sectors, when the green shoots emerge, Singapore could face a shortage of our top entrepreneurial and managerial talent, namely top business leaders who serve as the directors of businesses.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The personal consequence of insolvencies to the directors are severe.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This is because bank loans to SMEs generally require a personal guarantee and it is frequently born by the directors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The result is that for several years at least, directors of many firms – the leaders of these badly hit industries – will not be able to raise funds and take an active role to transform their sector again.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: There will be a whole lot of hurt coming our way.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For the business leaders facing imminent personal bankruptcy, it can be a soul-crushing process, a destruction of a lifetime of hard work.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For their families, it could mean changed lives forever, not to mention many years of financial distress.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For their workers, it may mean a period of hardship until new jobs can be found.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It is our duty, as Members of this House, to do more, to prevent and reduce the pain.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The underlining objective of both amendments to offer streamlined procedures for renegotiation, restructuring and potential termination of contracts, especially for smaller businesses, is well founded and both timely and pertinent in light of the disruptions introduced by the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I only wish to raise a few points – mainly on the scope of each Bill's coverage but also wish to take a step back and highlight the key big picture issues on the implications of a less onerous bankruptcy resolution regime for entrepreneurial culture, that the IRDA amendment Bill inevitably identifies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The realignment framework stipulates that contracts signed prior to COVID-19 be made available to possible renegotiation or termination with a moratorium period pertaining to affected agreements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is eminently sensible given the forced stoppage to economic activity imposed by the circuit breaker and other COVID-19 containment measures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Following Minister Desmond Lee's speech, my rusty Math now sees that it is basically four months.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But by my count, the circuit breaker and Phase One lasted for 73 days; while that of Phase One to the start of the Bill is 136 days.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One is left to wonder how this cap of four months was actually chosen, given that it is not closely related to the specific phases and disruption periods that were identified by policy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps more relevant, it is not so much the maximum number of days for which a delay is allowed but rather why there is no equivalent minimum.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Here, I am keenly aware that I always seems to be harping about minimums these days.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Importantly, while larger firms may well be able to accelerate their work schedules to meet or exceed unanticipated delays, smaller firms simply do not possess the economies of scale or scope to do so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, if delivery is possible within a shorter window so much the better.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But allowing for a default, returns some bargaining power back to the small businesses which were forced to disrupt activity due to no fault of their own.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The other benefit of such a default is that small and micro businesses that possess limited understanding of the realignment framework can easily grasp the principle that an automatic extension of the contract terms for the duration of the circuit breaker period applies via this default.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This brings me to the related issue of how small firms will navigate the complexities of revised legislation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In particular, sections 68 and 69 simultaneously remove the right of appeal while limiting the ability of assignees to obtain informed advice in the Adjustment Relief Assessment process.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While this stipulation can expedite what could well be a flood of assessments, it also presumes the accuracy of the official Assessor.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This introduces a clear asymmetry in the power dynamic between the two relevant parties.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps a potential route of appeal with an alternative, independent Assessor, applicable to special cases, could be considered.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At the very least, the circumstances by which the Adjustment Relief Assessor may permit the presence of legal representation should be spelled out.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As written, the IRDA Bill currently concurs significant discretion to the Executive to alter jurisdictional parameters by which the Act applies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In some instances, such discretion is well justified and increases operational flexibility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For instance, section 250F details specific eligibility criteria for firms' acceptance into the simplified winding up programme, but also allows for these values to be substituted by the Minister by order in the Gazette.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, in other instances, the discretion affords a very wide berth without clear justification for such leeway.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In particular, section 72H and 250H allows the Executive to freely overturn acceptance and eligibility requirements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This could open up avenues for potential error, thereby, undermining confidence in the application of the Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, the language of the Bill does not limit the authority only to the Minister but also to all political officerholders, such as the Second Minister, Minister of State or Senior Minister of State and the Parliamentary Secretary or Senior Parliamentary Secretary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I understand this allows secondary officeholders to act in the stead of the Minister should he or she be otherwise predisposed, we should be mindful that it also raises the risk of potential inconsistencies, as I have just shared.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Alternatively, the Minister could provide a clear public explanation for every waiver that is granted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As I alluded to previously, it is difficult to be certain ex ante whether the specific parameters used to define micro and small enterprises – the beneficiary targets of the IRDA Bill – are reasonable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I appreciate that the existing qualification criteria were not chosen in an arbitrary fashion, but it is also useful to recognise that the definitions for what constitutes a small enterprise differs worldwide.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And it would be a micro enterprise in Somalia.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, my point is not so much that definitions differ.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Relatedly, it may be worthwhile considering qualifications subject to simply just satisfying one or two, rather than the set of all criteria.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While it is important that such firms be allowed to fail when the economy is operating far below potential, as is likely the case in Singapore today, over zealous persecution could wipe out the income of the firm's erstwhile workers which would otherwise have been available to spend on the economy, which may end up in turn, prolonging the recession.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, it is also equally important that we understand what the trade-offs we are making are.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: On the flip side, there is substantial evidence that appropriately designed restructuring procedures can encourage entrepreneurship, especially for small business owners who would otherwise assume their firms' debts as personal liabilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Less onerous insolvency legislation can also promote opportunity-seeking and innovation orientation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As we transition our economy towards a knowledge and information-driven one, the continued refinement of IRDA would play an important role in cultivating a culture that is more willing to take on calculated business risks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Whether we decide on permanently codifying the temporary measures introduced by the IRDA amendment Bill, then lies in our assessment of whether these reforms are deemed to have fulfilled their objective of improving the business climate for small and medium enterprises – not just during this COVID-19 period, but beyond.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To that end, it is imperative that we embed the tools to evaluate the efficacy of the law even as we begin to roll it out in earnest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At the simplest level, this would entail complimentary collection of relevant data on firms that avail themselves to the simplified regime versus those that decline it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In a similar spirit, more systematic sector-by-sector tracking of the performance of small firms deploying further provisions should also be undertaken.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The amendments taken together is a holistic approach as the Bills are complementary and reinforce each other to assist small and micro businesses.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: However, we must keep in mind the reality that some micro and small businesses will never recover.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The good part, Mdm Deputy Speaker, is that my understanding is that these Bills are essentially for these entities to elect.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: So, I am a bit confused when the hon Member Jamus Lim spoke about the challenges in terms of the use of independence and additional lawyers to support the move to essentially recover from the challenges posed by the pandemic for these small and micro businesses.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The existing insolvency process today, while useful, takes time and is expensive.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: And in this case, the amendment allows more than micro businesses that are already struggling and cannot afford more costs.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As such, the SIP is a welcome response to meet the urgent needs under this pandemic condition.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: That is why I said, it is an option and Small and Micro businesses that do not feel that it benefits them, need not move and elect for these remedies in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I now turn to the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) (Amendment No 3) Bill.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The intent is to help eligible businesses impacted by this pandemic to focus on the future and not be stuck in unproductive positions is a positive move.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: On this, I wish to raise three areas: two on the eligibility criteria and the third on how the current Bill works with the rental relief framework, that will impact the effectiveness and execution of the Bill, for Minister's consideration and clarification.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: On the eligibility criteria, the use of (a) revenue drop to identify businesses impacted and (b) business size to ringfence this remedy for smaller companies is logical.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: However, I would request the Minister to ensure that such interventions are well calibrated to ensure a balanced and fair approach to all businesses.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The reason for this is that our Government must advocate for our businesses that sit on both sides of the contract.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: A clear example would be in the area of leases, where there is a clear need to take care of not just tenants, but also landlords.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: So, there is a need minimise interference in the risk-taking between parties that is at the heart of business activities and the spirit of entrepreneurship.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In the example of a successful small businesses in the F&B industry, with a healthy 30% profit margins last year, this means that with a 30% drop in revenue this year, the business would already be bottom-line break-even.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Under this pandemic situation, small businesses operating at half of its previous turnover is not uncommon.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This means that a high revenue drop eligibility criteria requirement would be of little assistance to businesses that are already struggling.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Further to the above, I also seek the Minister's consideration on calibrating reliefs for certain agreements.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I believe that for example, tenants that are stuck in fixed rental lease agreements are in greater need of the present reliefs tabled compared to those leases which vary with the turnover of the tenant.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Regardless of what the eligibility criteria might be, this amendment Bill might potentially have a negative impact on some businesses that narrowly miss the threshold.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I think Minister gave some examples earlier on and these examples are not unlikely to happen, where in the case of a tenant-landlord relationship, as an example, it is probable that the position of a landlord of a non-eligible business might harden.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: He may be emboldened not to negotiate as the landlord would be aware that the tenant will not be eligible to terminate his lease without incurring sizeable penalties.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This can potentially happen, which runs contrary to the good intentions of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I now turn to the last part, which is my query on the interoperability of the earlier rental relief framework and the present framework.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that there have been businesses that have availed themselves to the rental relief framework but have continued to perform poorly and have been incurring substantial financial losses.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Such businesses now may wish to then invoke the reliefs under the present framework to exit their businesses notwithstanding the previous assistance they had benefited from.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In concluding, Mdm Deputy Speaker, the Bills represent a proactive step by the Government, which I believe will be welcomed by the public.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It is tough to find the exact balance to avoid under or over-correction.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Under-correcting will lead to helping fewer deserving entities, while over-correcting will distort the market.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: But we cannot fear to act, to do the right thing.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, the courage that I spoke about earlier of the Government and Second Minister for Law for tabling these Bills.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many businesses, including our MSCs, may not be able to weather this storm.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If they are to survive, they may need significant restructuring.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill recognises the reality that the experiences of MSCs facing restructuring or winding up are going to be very different from that of companies with more substantial assets.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I commend the effort to streamline the processes for MSCs that are in this position.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also support the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) (Amendment No 3) Bill which addresses difficulties faced by another group – companies in our construction sector.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three points of clarification for the IRDA Bill and one point on the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) (Amendment No 3) Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The threshold is important because a company that is able to continue without intervention should not be forced to undergo restructuring at the whims of a small number of creditors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Restructuring may also compromise the rights of creditors, including those that vote against approving it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To ensure that we strike a correct balance, will Minister share what further safeguards are in place to help businesses in the face of potentially overzealous creditors?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Related to this, can Minister share what guidance is provided to MSCs and their creditors in deciding whether and when to undertake restructuring?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, I understand that Credit Counselling Singapore will administer the restructuring assistance scheme for sole proprietorships and partnerships.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister share if the Simplified Insolvency Scheme will be complemented by programmes that provide closer guidance for MSCs and their creditors through the restructuring process?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, the new subsection 50(1A) allows exempted individuals to hold an insolvency practitioner’s licence without being "a qualified person." The licensing regime for insolvency practitioners was introduced in the Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution Act 2018.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It was a welcomed move to increase professional standards in this area.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, allowing exemptions to basic qualifications required of insolvency practitioners, so soon after the new regime is in place to raise standards, might send a contradictory message on the expected standards of insolvency practitioners.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister clarify in what situations does the Ministry intend to use this exemption clause?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What checks and balance will be in place to ensure that exempted individuals perform to the standards expected?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, will exempted individuals be required to hold any basic qualifications?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister clarify if this exemption is intended to cope with the short-term increase in case-load from the fast-track process or is this intended to be a general longer term exemption?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister also share if exempted individuals will be provided with any guiding principles on how to apply the relevant insolvency principles in relation to winding up or restructuring?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will Minister explain what factors were taken into account when stipulating this specific duration of time?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will there be any possibility of the fast-track process being extended and what are the factors that determine this extension?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, the intention behind the Bill of allowing smaller companies to avoid the increased costs and time associated with the usual court process should continue to apply after we have emerged from this crisis.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will Minister therefore share if the Ministry will consider adopting the provisions of this Bill on a permanent basis for MSCs and possibly even all SMEs in the future?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For my final point, I turn to the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) (Amendment No 3) Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The universal extension of time is a welcomed move.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand there are currently some uncertainty on whether an extension of time automatically applies once a contractor has applied for relief from liquidated damages under Part 2, section 6 of the current Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As a practical safeguard, some contractors may be legally advised to continue applying for an extension of time pursuant to the contract provisions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, this gives rise to its own set of issues.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Importantly, an extension of time under the contract may be discretionary.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, condition precedents for the extension of time stated under the contract may not have been fulfilled.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand this is a common defence raised.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, contractors who require relief for a longer period of time may still have to seek recourse under part 2, section 6 or negotiate under their contract provisions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this event, can the Minister clarify whether an extension of time automatically applies where a contractor applies for relief and serves a Notification for Relief?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If so, can the Minister clarify how this extension of time beyond the four-month period interacts with the contract provisions on extension of time?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The intent of this programme is to provide a simplified process for eligible companies that require support, to: restructure their debts to rehabilitate the business, or wind up the company as the business has ceased to be viable.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In respect of a simplified winding up, the process is based on the voluntary winding up process, instead of a Court-ordered winding up, and removes the necessity of a Court application to place the company into winding up.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The simplified proceedings may help to reduce the time and costs involved in conventional insolvency processes which, in turn, may help to somewhat increase the overall pool of assets and monies to be eventually used to satisfy a company’s debts.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is something I have raised on several occasions in this House.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the event that a company has to wind up, even though there is a priority of debts provided in the Act, workers’ outstanding wages and salaries remain unsecured debts, which may result in a situation where there are little assets left to pay these workers’ salaries and benefits, including those provided in their collective agreements, after all the company’s secured debts have been satisfied.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the event the company survives and continues its operations, an unpaid worker may still need to go through a protracted enforcement process against the company to recover unpaid salaries and retrenchment benefits where provided and applicable.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Even then, there is no guarantee that the worker would be able to recover all his outstanding salary, retrenchment benefits or benefits under their collective agreement.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is further exacerbated during recent times when companies undergo insolvency or other related proceedings, such as judicial management and receivership.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In any event, there is little or no recourse for both workers and unions as a moratorium of sorts prohibits the enforcement of rights under a collective agreement or any other due process.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Although a leave of Court could be obtained, this has to be done through legal processes which may be too onerous, involve costs and, sometimes, beyond the reach of workers and unions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: A good example would be the latest announcement of the closure of Robinson's Department Store last Friday.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Robinson's is a branch of the Singapore Manual and Mercantile Workers’ Union for which I am their Executive Secretary.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The union is in talks with the management and the liquidators.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In fact, in this latest Robinson's saga which caught many unawares by the sudden closure, there are broadly three main groups that will be impacted.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is disconcerting that workers who stay on to help the company out of loyalty may be left with little or nothing at all.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Second, the SMEs and vendors that are in business with Robinson's.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Over the past few days, there have been several news reports quoting vendors who have come out to state that they have been unpaid for months.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is worrying, as it also signals a possible snowball effect, where a company not duly paid and, therefore, has its business viability threatened which, ultimately, may lead to unintended impact and consequences on the livelihoods of workers employed in these SMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Third, not to forget the many Robinson's customers who have bought and paid for items but have yet to receive those items, who now have to deal with the liquidators and left in the lurch.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is laudable that the Bill seeks to help companies and businesses by simplifying and expediting relevant insolvency proceedings during these difficult economic times.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, in the same vein, many workers have had their livelihoods impacted in this period of economic uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Hence, there should also be more direct assistance provided to support workers who seek to recover their unpaid wages, salaries or benefits by simplifying and expediting the enforcement of recovery proceedings.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is especially pertinent where the employer companies are experiencing financial difficulties and there are limited assets to satisfy all creditors.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: By the same token, vendors that have business with the company as well as consumers should also be accorded some form of protection in such scenarios.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We are in challenging times and the introduction of this No 3 Bill and its attendant initiatives are laudable.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This new Bill provides for contracts already entered into, to be renegotiated.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is something novel amidst these unprecedented and uncertain times.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Renegotiation would aid businesses to survive the brunt of this downturn, as many of them had entered into contracts when the outlook was very different.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The pricing model and assumptions as to costs were also quite different.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The survivability of companies and businesses also has ramifications for jobs and workers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Since April, we have been responding well to these consequences and must continue to do so because the months ahead will continue to be challenging for our country and economy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: MinLaw has made strategic changes to our laws, thereby enabling Singapore to be highly adaptable and flexible, which is essential for our businesses.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many of these contracts were signed in one particular context.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This approach is extremely practical to ensure that Singapore’s legal framework for businesses continues to be responsive and competitive.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I strongly believe that Singapore needs to support our businesses by giving them the opportunity to re-start and the Re-Align Framework is certainly a tangible effort in that direction.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I hope that “Re-Align” signals the continuation of contracts with new commitments, rather than an immediate termination of contracts.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We hope that these renegotiations lead to a continuation of the existing contract with new and acceptable obligations so that businesses grow with certainty, thereby protecting jobs and livelihoods of our Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This offers mental wellness for our entrepreneurs that old debts are managed.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They can focus quickly on restarting their businesses, creating jobs and contributing to the overall economy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Regarding the amendments made to both Bills, I have two considerations and two clarifications that I would like to put forward to MinLaw.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One of my considerations is to urge the Ministry to set evaluation criteria that would cover a large majority of companies, so that the intent of the amendment is broadly achieved.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On my second consideration, I would like to recommend providing other types of qualifying criteria other than aggregate group revenue, such as EBITA, as companies in the same industry may have different cost and margin compositions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, a $4 million revenue grossing furniture retail company will have different profitability and employment sizes, compared to a $4 million grossing electronics retail company.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Adding to this point, I would like to further propose having a different qualifying criteria for different industries, as businesses in different industries have varied margins and the ability to withstand shocks.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, a $50 million grossing company in pharmaceuticals is very different from one in services.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, additional evaluation criteria, other than revenue, recognises intra-industry nuances, and an industry-specific approach to recognise inter-industry differences, will help to save businesses and jobs effectively.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On my clarifications, firstly, I would like to ask if the framework could include sunk costs by tenants, such as exhaust system, M&E systems, fire suppression systems to offset outstanding obligations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is because such fixtures could eventually benefit the landlord in the event of a contract termination.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The landlord in this case would have a fitted-out unit to lease.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If so, most companies would not have audited accounts for the period in 2020.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When both parties approach with such a rational and progressive mindset, the amendments to these Bills can be very successful in helping all parties navigate through these tough times.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With such adaptable and flexible approaches by the Ministry, I believe tough businesses will outlast tough times.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I would first like to declare that I am a practising lawyer, a director in a law practice involved in dispute resolution work, a member of the Law Society of Singapore and the co-chairperson of the Law Society's Pro Bono Services' Community Legal Clinics' Committee.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Over the past few months, we have witnessed how the COVID-19 pandemic has wrecked economic devastation on our people.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It would be an understatement to say that many Singaporeans are badly affected by these economic difficulties and that it would be a long cold winter ahead for many more.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The small and micro businesses are the backbone of our economy, many of which have the potential to continue their businesses despite the on-going pandemic by adopting new practices.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, there are still more that are suffering.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For instance, the night-life industry and travel and tourism-related businesses are still struggling due to their inability to resume operations, causing them to experience a tremendous drop in revenue while their financial obligations continue unabated.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The owner of one of the buffet restaurants that catered mainly to tourists during pre-COVID-19 days had shared with me recently that while he is appreciative of the Government's grants and support systems that we have offered, his business continues to suffer and struggle with revenue as his customer pool has dwindled.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, his business operation costs have only gone up while the arrears in rental fees continue to accrue.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For the past few months, many residents have either written to me or met me at the Meet-the-People Sessions to enquire about the legal issues that they are facing.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There are two relevant scenarios that I would like to take this opportunity to share with this House.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: She wrote to me expressing her concern about the debts that she has been owing as a result of the failing business.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is clear that the persons in both scenarios continue to suffer from the pandemic's effects, whether it be worrying about one's business or how to enforce their rights as a landlord in this trying time.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Upon perusing the Bills, I am heartened that these situations stated therein are applicable to the two scenarios concerning my residents, which I have shared earlier and will, hopefully, put them at great ease.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With that said, I would like to ask a few questions about the execution of the two Bills.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Just like SIRS, I anticipate that the Re-Align Framework will invite much interest and many applications by business owners whose businesses have been adversely affected as a result of this unexpected COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How will the Ministry ensure that the assessor panels are adequately staffed so as to be responsive to the applications made within a short time period?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While the realigned framework and SIP are beneficial, we need to raise awareness to ensure that those eligible will know how to apply and are encouraged to do so.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this regard, what assistance, including legal assistance, will be provided to help these businesses understand their options and to advise them on whether and how to invoke the right framework or programme?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Under what circumstances will permission be actually granted by the assessor?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The general perception is that engaging a lawyer equates to hefty costs and protracted proceedings.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In recent years, at the Courts' encouragement and with the support of the Law Society of Singapore, the role of lawyers have begun to shift towards facilitating disputes to be resolved amicably between parties without resorting to lengthy litigious Court proceedings.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I take the position that we should recognise that lawyers should still be allowed to play a vital role in the execution of the two Bills.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Lawyers can advise and ensure that both the applicant and respondent follow the correct rules and procedures and draft the necessary documents required – and not just pertaining to what Assoc Prof Jamus Lim has suggested earlier in the House to include a course of appeal and for legal representation to be granted for the appeal proceeding.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I have also had the privilege to speak to contractors and sub-contractors and visit construction sites that are in the midst of restarting construction activities.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, I have had a first-hand glimpse into the extent of disruption that the COVID-19 pandemic has caused to the construction and property sectors.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: With regard to MND's proposed amendments to the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) Act to provide further relief to the built environment sector, I would like to raise three points.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: While I welcome the move, anecdotally, it has not been easy in the first place for contractors and other players to fully account for the additional costs caused by the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: For example, movement restrictions mean their supervisors who are on S Pass and with lodging outside the dormitories now have to take private transport.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Thirdly, also on the universal extension of time, I would like to recognise that for most industry players, the disruption caused by COVID-19 has gone well beyond four months.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I hope the Ministry has consulted the industry widely for this proposed amendment and has achieved broad buy-in.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It would also help the industry if potentially disruptive safe management measures like the quarantining of workers could be applied more consistently.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: There has been feedback about apparent inconsistencies on the ground whereby some workers get quarantined but others in similar circumstances do not.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: That said, I know our officers implementing these measures have been working very hard and trying their level best.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In this respect, I hope the BluePass tokens for targeted contact tracing amongst the construction worker community will be a game-changer.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Ultimately, these measures, while potentially disruptive, reflect a new normal that the industry must adapt to in order to resume construction activities safely.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The additional pain will persist but our construction industry is rising to the occasion.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: As long as everyone continues to play its part and share the burden, we will get through this together.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):   COVID-19 has dealt a severe blow to the construction and the property sectors.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The numerous measures introduced by the Government have prevented a total collapse of these sectors.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The immediate challenge will be to help businesses recover slowly under the new normal.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: By adopting this two-pronged approach, the Government will help businesses tide over this difficult time and emerge stronger.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a testimony to the intense efforts that have been put in by the whole-of-Government to help Singapore and Singaporeans as well as Singapore businesses navigate through this crisis.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a point that the hon Member Mr Edward Chia just made a few minutes ago.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The fact that we have been able to move speedily to consider and, if found appropriate, implement these legislative measures to provide the adaptation and scaffolding necessary for our businesses to climb out of the economic difficulties they face is commendable and sometimes can be taken for granted, but it should not be so.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In his speech, the hon Minister outlined the reasons why he believes the economic outlook is not likely to change in the near term.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Amongst the potential beneficiaries under the framework would be Mdm Prabha who is one of my residents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She runs a mini-mart from a rented premise.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She informs that before COVID-19, she was already impacted by dropping profits brought about by changing habits of residents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Since COVID-19 struck, she has not made a profit because the footfall dropped even further.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She now has a serious cash flow problem arising from her commitments to her vendors and landlord based on pre-COVID-19 contracts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Another resident of mine who may potentially benefit from this framework is Mr Andrew Neoh.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He is a blind masseur who rented premises to run his business.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He benefited from the rental relief introduced under "COVID 2".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, his business continues to decline and he is unable to meet his financial commitments under pre-COVID-19 lease.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For businesses run by people like Mdm Prabha and Mr Neoh, if we do not do anything, many small and micro businesses will fold and a lot more Singaporeans will be out of jobs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will exacerbate an already rising unemployment figures.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: No doubt, there will be a knock-on impact on families and society too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, there are implications for the future when SMEs fold leaving behind only the big players.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Senior Minister Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam identified this in an illuminating article entitled "The Global Jobs Crisis & Why We Should Think Longer Term" that was published in Straits Times on 31 October 2020.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He said, and I quote, "We need strategies to ensure that the SME sector survives and adapts to the new post-pandemic normal, to avoid much larger job losses in time as well as greater wage inequalities...While a churn of businesses is inevitable and needed, there is a real risk of a diminished SME sector as a whole, compounding the increases in industry concentration seen over the last few decades in many economies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That trend if it continues will have implications for future economic vibrance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It will likely also have an intangible impact on social capital." Currently, it would be difficult for small and micro-businesses to be able to lawfully terminate the pre-COVID-19 contracts without adverse consequences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As the hon Minister pointed out, firstly, they need to go to Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This would mean that they have to raise funds to instruct lawyers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is, in itself, a bridge too far for many of them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They would have to invoke the doctrine of frustration.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under this doctrine, a contract may be discharged if an unexpected supervening event makes it impossible for the contract to be performed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As the hon Minister pointed out, whilst the COVID-19 pandemic is an unanticipated supervening event, the economic consequence and significance on each individual contract is likely to differ.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given that the Courts apply this doctrine strictly, it would be difficult to predict whether it can be raised successfully.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Disputes arising from these matters will be referred to the assessor for final determination quickly.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a much better option for small and micro businesses.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do appreciate that some counterparties may feel aggrieved over this arrangement.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister dealt with this point in his speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Apart from the point that he made that these micro businesses are already financially distressed, I would add further that the ability to negotiate a contract would actually provide a win-win situation or at least have a potential to provide a win-win situation, given these market conditions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have two questions and two suggestions for the hon Minister.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, there is a need to properly categorise the SMEs that may invoke the relief measures under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And this is a point that a number of hon Members who spoke before me also raised.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As this is an important decision, I would imagine that the hon Minister would have already conducted some consultation with industry players before determining the figures.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Member Mr Edward Chia suggested having bespoke figures for each industry.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Whichever way the hon Minister decides, it is inevitable that there will be SMEs which will fall out of the criteria.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wonder if the hon Minister could please recount relief measures that these SMEs may be entitled even though they may not directly benefit from this Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, may I please ask whether, under this Bill, there is any provision that can be invoked to allow for the preservation of the status quo or restrain in exercising security rights whilst the process contemplated under the Bill is being played out?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would it not be consistent with the objective of the Bill for a hiatus to be built in so that the small and micro-businesses will not suffer further hardship through the exercise of security rights, for example, forfeiting deposits or security bonds?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Otherwise, the re-negotiation may take place in circumstances where the bargaining position of the small and micro businesses will be further weakened.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note that SMEs are encouraged to re-negotiate the contracts with the counterparties during the negotiation phase.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To facilitate these negotiations, may I please suggest that MinLaw make available to these parties some model clauses that they can incorporate into their revised contracts?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will have an impact of promoting certainty and enforceability of these revised contracts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, I wish to convey a suggestion mooted by my hon friend, Ms Nadia Samdin, in a pre-debate discussion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We should not assume that people who would benefit from this framework would be actively looking out for these matters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Such a proactive approach will augment the policy intent behind this Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They have been working in overdrive for some time now, all with a view to ensure that Singaporeans get the best help possible whilst we navigate ourselves out of this terrible crisis.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Re-Align Framework is unique and creative; a first in the annals of Singapore's legal history.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To them, this House and fellow Singaporeans owe them a debt of gratitude.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, Mr Louis Ng asked whether an EOT, beyond four months automatically applies when a contractor serves a Notification for Relief under Part 2 of the Act, and how this would interact with contractual provisions on EOT; while Assoc Prof Jamus Lim asked why we chose four months universal EOT instead of aligning with the two months circuit breaker or with Phase One, and Mr Xie Yao Quan asked if we had consulted the industry on the universal EOT proposal, and whether contracts between contractors and sub-contractors will also be covered.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, let me assure the Members that our proposals were developed in close consultation with the industry and are supported by the industry associations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As I mentioned earlier, two months account for the Circuit Breaker period, and two months account for the subsequent period when all dormitories were yet to be cleared.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, instead of aligning it with Phase One, we aligned it with the reality on the ground which is the duration for which most of the workers were still in the dormitories and the dormitories had not yet been cleared.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Contractors seeking an EOT beyond the universal four months period provided by the Bill should negotiate with their counter-party, or rely on contract provisions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The intent is to arrive at an amicable resolution that is acceptable to both parties.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But if the matter cannot be resolved, then the contractor can serve a Notification for Relief under the existing Part 2 of the Act.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Once the Notification for Relief is served, the contractor will be able to rely on the defence under section 6 of the Act against any claims for liquidated damages payable under the contract in respect of delays that are materially caused by COVID-19 which occur beyond the four months EOT provided by Part 8A, and within the prescribed period.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In this respect, in response to Mr Louis Ng's question, the protection afforded under section 6 of the Act is similar in effect to an EOT but they are not exactly identical.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For instance, depending on the terms of the contract, an EOT may clearly have an impact on matters such as defects liability period or DLP of a project.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Xie Yao Quan also asked how equitable co-sharing between parties will be determined in respect Part 8B of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: He suggested that we model the universal provision for co-sharing after the approach that has been adopted for public sector projects.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I think he is referring to the prolongation cost that the Government procuring entities have provided to Government projects.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Xie also said that it may not be easy for contractors to fully account for additional costs such as incremental private transport costs, which may add up.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To clarify, the provisions under Part 8B of the Bill provide for co-sharing of additional costs due to delays arising from COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have separately provided construction firms with substantial financial support to help with additional compliance costs associated with COVID-Safe restart criteria.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The first is to reiterate that these measures have to be looked at in the context of the broader schemes, measures, budgetary as well as non-fiscal measures that have been put in place to assist individuals, businesses and also to seek to rejuvenate the economy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And to the extent that Mr Henry Kwek has said what else can we do, and also whether we should keep and extend Part 3 of the earlier COVID Bill – please also look at this in the context of the fact that beyond these immediate measures, there are also measures implemented by MAS, by EDB.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There is the Extended Support Scheme, both standard and customised for those who do not meet within this scheme.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, all three of these Bills need to be looked at in tandem.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Some are complementary and, indeed, an individual or a business can use more than one of these measures.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I believe it was Mr Edward Chia who asked whether these are in addition to the measures that have been put in place in the earlier rental relief framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They do support the businesses who may already have enjoyed the rental relief framework but now choose to decide that they wish to renegotiate the contract with parties; you can avail yourself of this but, obviously, to the extent that the rental relief framework also provides for a repayment period, if the repayment schedule for the outstanding amounts has not been fulfilled, then it could be unfair to allow you to exit from the contract.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, that has to be taken into account.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Those arrears should be discharged and then you can look at the termination provisions under this plan.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Third, the purpose behind these measures, as I said at the start, is to rejuvenate, not only to look at where we were six months ago which was to hold the line with a moratorium.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That was the reason behind "COVID 1"; then with "COVID 2" we look at an additional injection to help tenants with their rental, one of the biggest cost components.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But we want to also look forward, in terms of rejuvenation so, for example, I mentioned we do not want to have zombie companies remain on the books, companies which are no longer sustainable as a business entity, but which remains alive because of financial and fiscal injection.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is not going to be viable in the long term.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It ties up resources, manpower as well as assets.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We also want to move away from the thresholds that just hold the line.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
